Q: knuth multiplicative hash A:

The accepted answer uses this code:

uint32_t hash(uint32_t v)
{
    return v * UINT32_C(2654435761);
    // do not comment about the lack of right shift. I'm not ignoring it. read on.
}

While the argument about the lack of right shift is correct, this implementation may be incorrect for some architectures. Let's analyze step by step.

Both operands of the multiplication have type uint32_t and, depending on the architecture, we have multiple possibilities:

  • if int has 31 value bits (the most common case, width is 32), type uint32_t is probably the same as unsigned int, no integer promotion is performed and the multiplication is performed using unsigned int arithmetics, ie: no overflow, result has type unsigned int and has the expected value, the conversion to the return type is a no-op.

  • if int has fewer than 31 value bits (eg: a width of 16 or 24 bits), uint32_t is a type larger than unsigned int, either type unsigned long or an extended type. No promotion is performed and in the first case, the multiplication is performed modulo ULONG_MAX and the result has the expected value and the conversion to the return type is a no-op. In the second case, the behavior is implementation defined as the type is an extended type, but the result should have the expected value after conversion.

  • if int has more than 31 value bits (has a width greater than 32), then both operands are promoted to int and the multiplication is performed using signed arithmetics. Again 2 possibilities:

    • if int has at least 64 value bits (has a width greater than 64) then the result will fit in an int and the conversion to the return type uint32_t is fully defined and will produce the expected result, ie: the low 32-bits of the multiplication result. A smart compiler should generate optimal code for this using a 32-bit multiplication opcode. I have never seen or heard of an actual architecture where int has a width larger than 64, apart from a hypothetical DS9K variant.
    • if int has 64 value bits or less, the multiplication may overflow (eg: v = UINT32_MAX) and the behavior is undefined. So this solution is inappropriate for architectures where int has 64 bits, and such architectures are possible (rare, but do exist).

Note that the macro UINT32_C is not fully portable: is was introduced in C99, but then so was the type uint32_t so restricting this implementation to C99 seems acceptable.

The problem remains for architectures with a 64-bit int type (or a width between 33 and 64 bits) for which the behavior is undefined in many cases.

We can solve this simply by using 2654435761U instead of UINT32_C(2654435761): the type of 2654435761U is either unsigned int if int has a width of at least 32 or unsigned long on architectures with a smaller int type. This ensures that the multiplication is always performed using unsigned arithmetics, so its behavior is always defined, and the result is always truncated (if necessary) when converted to the return type.

Here is the modified version, which illustrates a cardinal principle: simplicity kills!

uint32_t hash(uint32_t v)
{
    return v * 2654435761U;
}

Q: How do I start building a custom AOSP-based OS for a POS device? A:

The OS will run only on dedicated POS hardware.

Do you know what chipset it has and the BSP support from the ODM? That would define long term longevity.

Users should not be able to install arbitrary applications from APK files, Google Play, or other sources.

This is possible to achieve in the framework / system apps layer.

I want to customize the boot process and possibly use a custom bootloader.

Every device has it's own boot process - dependent on the chipset / ODM. What are you trying to achieve?

The device should boot directly into my POS application (kiosk mode).

It is possible to make a certain app the Home app and hide the system bars, etc.

System settings should be restricted so users cannot modify important configurations.

You could develop your own Settings app with limited options.

I may need remote updates for the OS and the POS application.

It is possible to implement the an Updater app which provides support for application and OS updates. You would also need to have a backend and deployment control based on certain policies.

I would like to remove unnecessary Android components to reduce the attack surface and improve performance.

This is a very broad requirement but one could start somewhere like Secure Boot, etc., but all depend on the kind of hardware being exposed and then software specific hardening may be possible too. The fastest way is to be compliant with the ASB and vendor updates.

Q: Element in BoxLayout kivy A:

from kivy.app import App

from kivy.uix.boxlayout import BoxLayout

from kivy.uix.label import Label

from kivy.uix.button import Button

import random

class CasinoGame(BoxLayout):

def \__init_\_(self, \*\*kwargs):

    super().\__init_\_(orientation='vertical', \*\*kwargs)

    self.label = Label(text="آماده بازی هستی؟", font_size='30sp')

    self.add_widget(self.label)

    

    self.btn = Button(text="چرخش اسلات")

    self.btn.bind(on_press=self.spin)

    self.add_widget(self.btn)

def spin(self, instance):

    symbols = \["🍒", "🍋", "🔔", "⭐", "7"\]

    result = \[random.choice(symbols) for \_ in range(3)\]

    self.label.text = " | ".join(result)

    

    if result\[0\] == result\[1\] == result\[2\]:

        self.label.text += "\\nجک‌پات! برنده شدی!"

class MyApp(App):

def build(self):

    return CasinoGame()

if _name_ == '_main_':

MyApp().run()

Q: MERN stack user registration form not working A:

You need to pass complete url in fetch instead of just /signup.

Assuming you're running your app on local server and on port 4000, endpoint you should be hitting is http://localhost:4000/signup

Simply update your fetch method to this

// Send the form data to the backend
fetch('http://localhost:4000/signup', {
  method: 'POST',
  body: formData,
})

Check this for cors error

How to solve CORS request did not succeed in express.js when react client try fetch data?

Q: Set extended keys for Vaydeer macro keypad A:

Here you will find my project to customize the Vaydeer keypad:

https://github.com/philipp-fischer/vaydeer-macro-keyboard

It also contains a tutorial on how to build and flash a firmware that supports F13-F24 keys, the ideal AHK2 keys to use for custom macros.

If you are more interested in how the Vaydeer configuration and firmware flashing works, the repo also contains some in-depth information on that.

Q: how to restore default setting in postman A:

Previous to restore default settings.

Sign out of Postman: When Sign out of Postman it removes your synced history, collections and environments from local storage.

Otherwise when you re-install it, it is likely that it'll use the old data from the previous installation.
